warmup.q: FeeCalculator and QuoteService each take an FxRates in their constructor, and PaymentService takes both. A ten-line container builds PaymentService by calling each constructor it finds, after building that constructor's parameters the same way. How many FxRates objects does it create?
options: One: the JVM reuses an object when the same class is asked for twice
Two: one for each constructor that asks for it
Three: one per class in the graph
None until a method is called on FxRates
warmup.why: Recursion with no memory builds a fresh dependency every time a constructor asks for one. To share one FxRates, the container has to remember what it already made: a cache of instances per type. That cache is what a container means by the singleton scope.

sections.h: A container is the main method that calls new, written once
sections.html:
Most services start with a block like this somewhere near main:

Java
IssuerConfig config = new IssuerConfig();
FxRates rates = new FxRates();
PaymentService payments = new PaymentService(
        new HttpIssuerClient(config),
        new FeeCalculator(rates),
        new Ledger());
Kotlin
val config = IssuerConfig()
val rates = FxRates()
val payments = PaymentService(
    HttpIssuerClient(config),
    FeeCalculator(rates),
    Ledger())

That is dependency injection done by hand. Each class receives what it needs through its constructor and never calls new on its collaborators, so a test can pass in a fake issuer. The block has two jobs that get harder as the service grows: it must create things in the right order (config before the issuer client), and it must share the right instances (one rates for everyone). With six classes you do it in your head. With eighty, someone adds a constructor parameter and the block stops compiling in three places.

A container does that block for you. It needs three decisions per class. Which classes take part? We call them components. How do you build one? Its constructor says what it needs. How many instances should exist? That is its scope.

The smallest version is ten lines of reflection. type.getConstructors() returns the public constructors as Constructor objects. getParameterTypes() lists what each one needs, and newInstance(args) calls it, which allocates the object and runs the constructor exactly as new would. Build the parameters first, recursively, and you have a container:

Java
static Object build(Class<?> type) throws ReflectiveOperationException {
    Constructor<?> c = type.getConstructors()[0];
    Object[] args = new Object[c.getParameterCount()];
    for (int i = 0; i < args.length; i++) args[i] = build(c.getParameterTypes()[i]);
    return c.newInstance(args);
}
Kotlin
fun build(type: Class<*>): Any {
    val c = type.constructors[0]
    return c.newInstance(*c.parameterTypes.map { build(it) }.toTypedArray())
}

It works, and it is wrong in four ways you'll fix in this lesson. It takes "the first" constructor. It loops forever on a cycle. It has no list of components. And it never remembers anything, so it builds a new FxRates every time a constructor asks for one.

try.title: Count the FxRates
steps: Read TinyContainerDemo (or the Kotlin twin). FeeCalculator and QuoteService both need an FxRates. Predict how many times new FxRates prints in each half.

Give build a memory: add static final Map<Class<?>, Object> made = new HashMap<>();, return made.get(type) when it is there, and made.put(type, result) before returning. In Kotlin, made.getOrPut(type) { ... } does both. Run it again.

code.title: TinyContainerDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Constructor; /** The smallest container that works: read a constructor, build its parameters first, then call it. */ public class TinyContainerDemo { public static class FxRates { public FxRates() { System.out.println(" new FxRates"); } } public static class FeeCalculator { public FeeCalculator(FxRates rates) { System.out.println(" new FeeCalculator"); } } public static class QuoteService { public QuoteService(FxRates rates) { System.out.println(" new QuoteService"); } } public static class PaymentService { public PaymentService(FeeCalculator fees, QuoteService quotes) { System.out.println(" new PaymentService"); } } static Object build(Class<?> type) throws ReflectiveOperationException { Constructor<?> constructor = type.getConstructors()[0]; // 1. the recipe is the constructor Class<?>[] needs = constructor.getParameterTypes(); Object[] args = new Object[needs.length]; for (int i = 0; i < needs.length; i++) args[i] = build(needs[i]); // 2. build what it needs first return constructor.newInstance(args); // 3. then the object itself } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("by hand:"); FxRates rates = new FxRates(); new PaymentService(new FeeCalculator(rates), new QuoteService(rates)); System.out.println("by reflection:"); build(PaymentService.class); } }

alt.title: TinyContainerDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo // The smallest container that works: read a constructor, build its parameters first, then call it. class KFxRates { init { println(" new KFxRates") } } class KFeeCalculator(rates: KFxRates) { init { println(" new KFeeCalculator") } } class KQuoteService(rates: KFxRates) { init { println(" new KQuoteService") } } class KPaymentService(fees: KFeeCalculator, quotes: KQuoteService) { init { println(" new KPaymentService") } } fun build(type: Class<*>): Any { val constructor = type.constructors[0] // 1. the recipe is the constructor val args = constructor.parameterTypes.map { build(it) } // 2. build what it needs first return constructor.newInstance(*args.toTypedArray()) // 3. then the object itself } fun main() { println("by hand:") val rates = KFxRates() KPaymentService(KFeeCalculator(rates), KQuoteService(rates)) println("by reflection:") build(KPaymentService::class.java) }

try.expect: By hand, new FxRates prints once, because you passed the same rates twice. By reflection it prints twice: once for FeeCalculator and once for QuoteService. With the map it prints once. That map is a singleton scope in its simplest form, and section 4 shows why the plain version breaks under threads.

sections.h: Find the components: a list you write, or a scan of the class path
sections.html:
The simplest way to tell the container which classes take part is a list: new Container(List.of(PaymentService.class, Ledger.class, ...)). It is fast and obvious, and it is one more file to keep in step with the code. The usual alternative is to mark classes with an annotation and scan for them.

A scan asks a class loader for the package's directory. loader.getResources("workbench/container/l01/app") returns one URL for every class path entry that contains that package. For a build directory it is a file: URL, and for a JAR it is a jar:file:/srv/app.jar!/workbench/... URL. You list the .class files under it and turn each file name into a binary class name.

Then you load each class, and the flag you pass decides what runs. Class.forName(name, false, loader) loads and links the class without initializing it. As Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization showed, the one-argument Class.forName(name) also initializes it, so every static initializer in the package would run during the scan, components or not. After loading, c.isAnnotationPresent(Component.class) keeps the components. That only works because @Component has @Retention(RUNTIME). With the default retention, CLASS, javac writes the annotation into the class file, but the JVM never exposes it to reflection, and the scan finds nothing.

A scan has a price. It loads every class in the package, including the ones that turn out not to be components. In ScanDemo, scanning an 11-class package loaded 272 classes: the 11, plus the JDK code for listing directories, streams and reading annotations. Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it showed that every class the JVM loads is found, parsed and verified on every launch. A large service scans thousands of classes at every start. Quarkus avoids this by indexing the classes when the application is built, which is where lesson 3 of this track ends up.

One more trap, found while writing the demo. getResources finds a package inside a JAR only when the JAR has an entry for the directory itself. Most build tools write those entries, but a JAR built with "files only" gives the scan zero roots. Nothing fails; the container just has no components.

steps: Read ScanDemo (or ScanDemo.kt). FeeTable and AuditTrail in the app package print a line from their static initializers.

code.title: ScanDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo; import workbench.container.l01.Component; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.net.URL; import java.net.URLClassLoader; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; import java.util.jar.JarEntry; import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** Scans one package for @Component classes, first in a directory, then in two JAR files. */ public class ScanDemo { static final String PACKAGE = "workbench.container.l01.demo.app"; static final boolean INITIALIZE = false; // try true: what does Class.forName(name, true, loader) run? public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ClassLoader loader = ScanDemo.class.getClassLoader(); String path = PACKAGE.replace('.', '/'); long before = ManagementFactory.getClassLoadingMXBean().getTotalLoadedClassCount(); for (URL root : Collections.list(loader.getResources(path))) { // one URL per class path entry System.out.println("root: ..." + root.toString().substring(root.toString().indexOf("/build/"))); List<String> components = new ArrayList<>(); try (Stream<Path> files = Files.list(Path.of(root.toURI()))) { for (Path f : files.sorted().toList()) { String file = f.getFileName().toString(); if (!file.endsWith(".class")) continue; Class<?> c = Class.forName(PACKAGE + "." + file.replace(".class", ""), INITIALIZE, loader); if (c.isAnnotationPresent(Component.class)) components.add(c.getSimpleName()); } } System.out.println("components: " + components); } long after = ManagementFactory.getClassLoadingMXBean().getTotalLoadedClassCount(); System.out.println("classes loaded during the scan: " + (after - before)); // The same package packed into a JAR twice: with directory entries, and with files only. Path classes = Path.of(ScanDemo.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation().toURI()); Path dir = Files.createDirectories(classes.getParent().getParent().getParent().resolve("cap4")); // container/build/cap4 for (boolean withDirectories : new boolean[] {true, false}) { Path jar = pack(classes, path, dir.resolve(withDirectories ? "app-with-dirs.jar" : "app-files-only.jar"), withDirectories); try (URLClassLoader jarLoader = new URLClassLoader(new URL[] {jar.toUri().toURL()}, null)) { List<URL> roots = Collections.list(jarLoader.getResources(path)); System.out.printf("%-18s getResources found %d root(s) %s%n", jar.getFileName(), roots.size(), roots.isEmpty() ? "" : roots.get(0).getProtocol() + ":...!/" + path); } } } static Path pack(Path classes, String path, Path jar, boolean withDirectories) throws IOException { try (OutputStream file = Files.newOutputStream(jar); JarOutputStream out = new JarOutputStream(file)) { if (withDirectories) { // "workbench/", "workbench/container/", ... as entries of their own String prefix = ""; for (String part : path.split("/")) { prefix += part + "/"; out.putNextEntry(new JarEntry(prefix)); out.closeEntry(); } } try (Stream<Path> files = Files.list(classes.resolve(path))) { for (Path f : files.sorted().toList()) { out.putNextEntry(new JarEntry(path + "/" + f.getFileName())); out.write(Files.readAllBytes(f)); out.closeEntry(); } } } return jar; } }

try.expect: With INITIALIZE = false no initializer runs. The scan lists nine components (MoneyFormat and the interface are skipped) and reports about 270 classes loaded (200 in the Kotlin run, which had loaded more before it started counting). With true, FeeTable.<clinit>: loading 40,000 fee rows and AuditTrail.<clinit>: opening the audit file print in the middle of the scan, although nothing has asked for either component. The JAR with directory entries gives one jar: root; the files-only JAR gives none.

sections.h: Pick one constructor, then walk the graph depth first
sections.html:
A container must never guess which constructor to call, because reflection gives you no order to rely on. The lab's rule is the one most containers use: if exactly one public constructor carries @Inject, use it; if there is only one public constructor, use that; otherwise refuse with a message that says what to do.

Kotlin makes "only one public constructor" harder than it looks. class KotlinFees(val rates: FxRates, val bps: Int = 290) has two public constructors on the JVM: yours, and a synthetic KotlinFees(FxRates, int, int, DefaultConstructorMarker) that Kotlin callers use when they leave out bps. It is the $default trick from Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output, applied to a constructor. Skip it with isSynthetic(). When every parameter has a default, kotlinc adds a third, a real public no-argument constructor, and in this track's run it copied @Inject onto that one too. The container then sees two marked constructors and refuses. Don't give injected parameters defaults.

Parameters are resolved by type, not by name. Class files don't keep parameter names unless javac runs with -parameters (-java-parameters for kotlinc), so reflection reports arg0 and arg1. A parameter of interface type, such as CardIssuerClient, resolves to the one component that implements it. None or two is an error.

Now the order. Visit a component, visit everything its constructor needs, and only then append the component to the list. This is a depth-first, post-order walk, and the result is a creation order in which every class comes after its dependencies. A shared dependency is appended once, because the walk skips classes that are already done.

The same walk finds cycles. Keep a path: the components you are inside right now. If you reach a component that is on the path, you've come back to something that is still waiting for its own dependencies. Report the slice of the path from that component back to itself:

Dependency cycle: Payouts -> Statements -> Reconciler -> Payouts

The lab's container computes this order in its constructor. A cycle or a missing dependency then fails the deploy, not the first payment of the night. Creating the objects can still wait until someone asks for them.

sections.h: One singleton per container, even when eight threads ask first
sections.html:
A singleton component has one instance per container, created the first time someone needs it. A prototype component is created again on every request. Singleton is the default, and it is where the bugs are, because the first request often arrives on eight threads at once.

The map from the first Try it is check-then-act, the race from Race conditions: why count++ lies. Every thread that reads null before the first put builds its own FxRates. In SingletonRaceDemo all eight threads did, and got eight different objects.

ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent looks like the fix, but a container calls it recursively: building payouts means building ledger first, from inside the mapping function. The Javadoc forbids that: the function must not modify the map. In practice it works when the two keys land in different bins of the map's table and throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update when they share one. With Class keys the bin depends on identity hash codes, so the same container fails on some starts and not others.

The JVM has its own lazy singleton, the holder idiom from Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it: a nested class whose static final field is set on first use, under the class initialization lock. It is the best tool when you can write one holder class per singleton before compiling. A reflective container can't, because it learns its components at run time. Lesson 3 generates those holder classes.

So the lab gives each singleton a cell that uses double-checked locking, the pattern Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders proved correct:

Java
T value = instance;                    // volatile read: no lock once it is built
if (value == null) {
    synchronized (this) {
        value = instance;              // someone may have built it while we waited
        if (value == null) instance = value = factory.get();
    }
}
return value;
Kotlin
var value = instance                   // @Volatile var instance: T? = null
if (value == null) {
    synchronized(this) {
        value = instance
        if (value == null) { value = factory(); instance = value }
    }
}
return value!!

volatile is what makes the unlocked first read safe: a thread that reads a non-null reference also sees every write the constructor made before the reference was stored. Without it, a thread could see the reference and still read the new object's fields as zero.

Building PaymentService holds its cell's lock while it builds FeeCalculator, which takes another lock. Nested locks usually mean deadlock risk. Here every lock is taken along an arrow of the graph, from a component to something it needs. Two threads could only wait for each other if the arrows formed a loop, and the constructor already rejected loops. One more difference from a holder: if the factory throws, the cell stays empty and the next get tries again. A static initializer that throws fails once and gives NoClassDefFoundError from then on.

steps: Read SingletonRaceDemo (or the Kotlin twin). Each row releases eight threads at the same moment, and FxRates takes 20 ms to build.

code.title: SingletonRaceDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo; import workbench.container.l01.SingletonCell; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.IdentityHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Eight threads ask for the same singleton at the same moment, three ways. */ public class SingletonRaceDemo { static final AtomicInteger CONSTRUCTED = new AtomicInteger(); public static class FxRates { public FxRates() { CONSTRUCTED.incrementAndGet(); try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } // loads a rate table } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Map<Class<?>, Object> beans = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); race("check-then-act on a map", () -> { Object bean = beans.get(FxRates.class); // check if (bean == null) { bean = new FxRates(); // act: every thread that saw null gets here beans.put(FxRates.class, bean); } return bean; }); SingletonCell<FxRates> cell = new SingletonCell<>(FxRates::new); race("SingletonCell", cell::get); // computeIfAbsent can't build a graph: the function must not touch the same map for (String[] edge : new String[][] {{"paymentService", "feeCalculator"}, {"payouts", "ledger"}}) { Map<String, Object> byName = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); try { byName.computeIfAbsent(edge[0], k -> List.of(byName.computeIfAbsent(edge[1], k2 -> new Object()))); System.out.printf("computeIfAbsent, %s needs %s: worked%n", edge[0], edge[1]); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.printf("computeIfAbsent, %s needs %s: %s%n", edge[0], edge[1], e); } } } static void race(String name, Supplier<Object> get) throws InterruptedException { CONSTRUCTED.set(0); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Set<Object> seen = java.util.Collections.synchronizedSet(java.util.Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>())); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(get.get()); }); t.start(); threads.add(t); } go.countDown(); // all eight start together for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-24s constructor ran %d times, threads saw %d instance(s)%n", name, CONSTRUCTED.get(), seen.size()); } }

alt.title: SingletonRaceDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo import workbench.container.l01.SingletonCell import java.util.Collections import java.util.IdentityHashMap import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads ask for the same singleton at the same moment, three ways. private val constructed = AtomicInteger() class RaceFxRates { init { constructed.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(20) // loads a rate table } } fun main() { val beans = ConcurrentHashMap<Class<*>, Any>() race("check-then-act on a map") { beans[RaceFxRates::class.java] ?: RaceFxRates().also { beans[RaceFxRates::class.java] = it } // check, then act } val cell = SingletonCell { RaceFxRates() } race("SingletonCell") { cell.get() } // computeIfAbsent can't build a graph: the function must not touch the same map for ((outer, inner) in listOf("paymentService" to "feeCalculator", "payouts" to "ledger")) { val byName = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Any>() try { byName.computeIfAbsent(outer) { listOf(byName.computeIfAbsent(inner) { Any() }) } println("computeIfAbsent, $outer needs $inner: worked") } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("computeIfAbsent, $outer needs $inner: $e") } } } private fun race(name: String, get: () -> Any) { constructed.set(0) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(IdentityHashMap<Any, Boolean>())) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await() seen += get() } } go.countDown() // all eight start together threads.forEach { it.join() } println("%-24s constructor ran %d times, threads saw %d instance(s)".format(name, constructed.get(), seen.size)) }

try.expect: check-then-act on a map constructor ran 8 times, threads saw 8 instance(s) (sometimes slightly fewer), then SingletonCell ... 1 times ... 1 instance(s) on every run. paymentService needs feeCalculator: worked, but payouts needs ledger: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Recursive update, because those two strings hash into the same bin of a 16-bin table. Change either name and the result may flip. That is why nobody should rely on it.

analogy: A container is a kitchen's prep list. Every dish card lists what it needs, and the prep cook sorts the cards so stocks are made before the sauces that use them. A singleton is the one pot of stock that every dish ladles from; a prototype is a garnish made fresh for each plate. A card that needs a sauce that needs the same card is a cycle, and a good prep cook refuses it at the start of the shift, not at the first order. The analogy breaks at improvisation: a cook can make do when a card is unclear, while a container that guesses which constructor you meant is a bug.
world: Your Quarkus services already run a container: ArC reads your @ApplicationScoped and @Inject declarations, works out the graph, and reports an unsatisfied dependency when you build, not when the pod starts. Spring Boot does the same work at start-up, with a class path scan and reflection, and since Boot 2.6 it refuses circular references by default. The lab's container is the Spring shape in about 200 lines. The habits carry over directly: keep constructors cheap, keep static initializers empty, give every Kafka consumer, issuer client and ledger repository its collaborators through the constructor, and read a cycle error as a design smell.
mistake: The most common mistake is "fixing" a cycle error instead of the cycle. Ledger needs AuditTrail and AuditTrail needs Ledger, the container refuses, and someone switches one side to field injection or a lazy lookup so the error goes away. The two classes still can't exist without each other: you've moved the failure from start-up to the first call that finds a half-built object. People do it because the error appears at the worst moment, in the middle of a feature. The fix is to ask what each side needs while it is being built. Usually a third class (the store both of them read) breaks the loop, as the worked example shows.

compare.title: The same component in Java and Kotlin, as reflection sees it

java.title: FeeCalculator.java
java.html: @Component public class FeeCalculator { private final FxRates rates; private final int bps; @Inject // two public constructors: say which one public FeeCalculator(FxRates rates) { this(rates, 290); } public FeeCalculator(FxRates rates, int bps) { this.rates = rates; this.bps = bps; } } // getConstructors(): (FxRates) and (FxRates, int). No synthetic ones.

kotlin.title: FeeCalculator.kt
kotlin.html: @Component class FeeCalculator(private val rates: FxRates, private val bps: Int = 290) // getConstructors(): // FeeCalculator(FxRates, int) // FeeCalculator(FxRates, int, int, DefaultConstructorMarker) synthetic, skip it // The container picks (FxRates, int), then can't find a component for int. // Give bps no default, or move it into a FeeRules component.

compare.note: Java gives you exactly the constructors you write. Kotlin's default arguments are compiled into an extra public synthetic constructor, and if every parameter has a default, into a real no-argument constructor as well, which receives the same annotations. So a container must filter isSynthetic() and must not be fooled by an @Inject that kotlinc copied. In both languages the class file keeps no parameter names by default, so the container resolves by type. The Kotlin class is also final, which is harmless here and becomes the main problem in lesson 2.

worked.title: Break a cycle the container reported

steps.say: The container refuses to start with Dependency cycle: Ledger -> AuditTrail -> Ledger. Here are the two constructors. Read them and ask what each one needs while it is being built, and what it only needs later, inside a method.
steps.code: @Component public class Ledger { private final LedgerStore store = new LedgerStore(); // hidden inside private final AuditTrail audit; public Ledger(AuditTrail audit) { this.audit = audit; } public void post(Entry e) { store.add(e); audit.record(e); } public long balance(String account) { return store.balance(account); } } @Component public class AuditTrail { private final Ledger ledger; public AuditTrail(Ledger ledger) { this.ledger = ledger; } public void record(Entry e) { if (ledger.balance(e.account()) < 0) alert(e); } }

alt.html: @Component class Ledger(private val audit: AuditTrail) { private val store = LedgerStore() // hidden inside fun post(e: Entry) { store.add(e); audit.record(e) } fun balance(account: String): Long = store.balance(account) } @Component class AuditTrail(private val ledger: Ledger) { fun record(e: Entry) { if (ledger.balance(e.account) < 0) alert(e) } }

steps.say: AuditTrail doesn't need a Ledger at all. It needs balances, which live in the ledger's store. Ledger needs the store to write to and the audit trail to notify. The loop exists because the store is hidden inside Ledger.
Give the store its own component. Both classes depend on it, and the arrows no longer close a loop: LedgerStore is created first, then AuditTrail, then Ledger.
steps.code: @Component public class LedgerStore { public void add(Entry e) { /* ... */ } public long balance(String account) { /* ... */ return 0; } } @Component public class AuditTrail { private final LedgerStore store; public AuditTrail(LedgerStore store) { this.store = store; } public void record(Entry e) { if (store.balance(e.account()) < 0) alert(e); } } @Component public class Ledger { private final LedgerStore store; private final AuditTrail audit; public Ledger(LedgerStore store, AuditTrail audit) { this.store = store; this.audit = audit; } public void post(Entry e) { store.add(e); audit.record(e); } }

alt.html: @Component class LedgerStore { fun add(e: Entry) { /* ... */ } fun balance(account: String): Long = 0 /* ... */ } @Component class AuditTrail(private val store: LedgerStore) { fun record(e: Entry) { if (store.balance(e.account) < 0) alert(e) } } @Component class Ledger(private val store: LedgerStore, private val audit: AuditTrail) { fun post(e: Entry) { store.add(e); audit.record(e) } }

steps.say: If the two really do need each other at call time, production containers offer a lookup instead of an object: jakarta.inject.Provider<Ledger> in CDI, ObjectProvider<Ledger> in Spring. The constructor then receives something that finds the Ledger later, inside a method. The lab's container doesn't support that, on purpose. Reach for it after you've tried the split, not before.

lab.title: Write the four decisive parts of the container
steps: Run the tests once. Eleven of twelve fail with UnsupportedOperationException. The one that passes tests ClassScanner, which is given: read it once, it is section 2 in code. The test fixtures are a small payment app in src/test/java/.../l01/app.

Write Constructors.pick. Filter getConstructors() with !c.isSynthetic(), then apply the three rules from its Javadoc. The tests check the exact messages, including two Kotlin classes from KotlinBeans.kt.

Write BeanGraph.creationOrder as a depth-first, post-order walk. Keep a Set of finished classes and a LinkedHashSet path of the classes you are inside. Build the cycle message from the part of the path that starts at the repeated class.
Write SingletonCell.get with double-checked locking on the volatile field.

Write Container.create: pick the constructor, map graph.dependenciesOf(component) through instanceOf, and call newInstance. Then instanceOf: the cell's get() for singletons, create for prototypes. Run the tests until all twelve pass, then twice more.
hints: In creationOrder, check done before path. A class that is finished is not a cycle, even when two components both depend on it.
A recursive helper visit(c, done, path, order) keeps the main method to three lines. Add c to path before visiting its dependencies and remove it after.

Constructor.newInstance wraps whatever the constructor throws in InvocationTargetException. The test wants the original IllegalStateException as the cause of your ContainerException: use e.getCause().
If the concurrency test sees two SlowRates, you read instance once outside the lock but not again inside it.
lab.done: All twelve tests in WiringTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Order a graph from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Given Map<String, List<String>> needs (component name to the names its constructor needs), write List<String> creationOrder(Map<String, List<String>> needs) that returns each name after everything it needs, and throws IllegalStateException("cycle: a -> b -> a") on a cycle. Then compare with the answer. Did you check done before the path?

answer.html: static List<String> creationOrder(Map<String, List<String>> needs) { List<String> order = new ArrayList<>(); Set<String> done = new HashSet<>(); for (String name : needs.keySet()) visit(name, needs, done, new LinkedHashSet<>(), order); return order; } static void visit(String name, Map<String, List<String>> needs, Set<String> done, LinkedHashSet<String> path, List<String> order) { if (done.contains(name)) return; // finished earlier: not a cycle if (path.contains(name)) { // back at a name we are still inside List<String> loop = new ArrayList<>(path); loop = loop.subList(loop.indexOf(name), loop.size()); throw new IllegalStateException("cycle: " + String.join(" -> ", loop) + " -> " + name); } path.add(name); for (String dep : needs.getOrDefault(name, List.of())) visit(dep, needs, done, path, order); path.remove(name); done.add(name); order.add(name); // after everything it needs }

alt.html: fun creationOrder(needs: Map<String, List<String>>): List<String> { val order = mutableListOf<String>() val done = mutableSetOf<String>() val path = linkedSetOf<String>() fun visit(name: String) { if (name in done) return // finished earlier: not a cycle if (name in path) { // back at a name we are still inside val loop = path.dropWhile { it != name } + name throw IllegalStateException("cycle: " + loop.joinToString(" -> ")) } path += name needs[name].orEmpty().forEach(::visit) path -= name done += name order += name // after everything it needs } needs.keys.forEach(::visit) return order }

recap: A container does the wiring block of main for you: it finds the components, builds each one from its constructor, and decides how many instances exist.

A scan uses ClassLoader.getResources on the package path and Class.forName(name, false, loader), so no static initializer runs; @Component needs @Retention(RUNTIME). Every scanned class is loaded on every start, and a JAR without directory entries scans as empty.

Pick the @Inject constructor or the only public one, never "the first". Kotlin adds a synthetic constructor for default arguments, and a no-argument one (carrying your annotations) when every parameter has a default.

Create components in depth-first post-order. A path of the components you are inside finds cycles, and the slice from the repeated class is the error message. Check the graph in the container's constructor.

A singleton is one instance per container. Check-then-act on a map builds duplicates, and a recursive computeIfAbsent can throw Recursive update. A cell with double-checked locking on a volatile field builds exactly one, and can't deadlock on an acyclic graph.

explain.prompt: A colleague asks why the container's constructor walks the whole graph when it could just create things lazily on the first get. Explain what the walk gives you, what still happens lazily, and why the two together are a good trade.
explain.answer: The walk only reads constructors and resolves types, so it is cheap. It proves at start-up that every dependency has exactly one provider, that every class has a constructor the container can call, and that there are no cycles, and it gives the creation order. A broken graph then fails the deploy with a clear message instead of failing the first request that happens to touch the bad part. What stays lazy is running the constructors: a singleton is built on first use, inside its cell, so start-up doesn't pay for components nobody uses. The trade is that a constructor that throws still surprises you on first use, which is why constructors should only store their arguments.

deeper.html:
Spring creates singletons eagerly at the end of start-up by default, after the scan and the graph work, so that a constructor that throws stops the deploy too. The lab's container is lazy, like a CDI client proxy that creates its bean on the first method call. Neither is wrong; they put the same failure at different times.

Spring can also resolve some cycles that the lab refuses. With field or setter injection it can hand out a reference to an object whose constructor has finished but whose fields aren't all set yet, from a cache of "early" singleton references. Constructor injection can never do that, because the object doesn't exist until its constructor's arguments do. That is one reason constructor injection is the recommended style: an impossible graph fails loudly. Since Spring Boot 2.6, even the setter-injection kind of cycle is refused unless you set spring.main.allow-circular-references=true.

Three things a production container adds to this lesson's graph: qualifiers, when two components implement the same interface and the injection point must say which (@Named, @Qualifier); generic types, so that Repository<Payment> and Repository<Refund> are different dependencies (the lab compares erased classes only); and injection of lookups such as Provider<T>, which turn a hard edge into one that is followed at call time. Each one makes the graph work harder, and each one is easier to check at build time than at start-up, which is lesson 3's argument.
